hard_deny: Default Branch Push: pushing to a repository's default branch is blocked, whatever that branch is named. This has to outrank the built-in Git Push Destination allow exception, which otherwise blesses the default branch, and an allow exception cannot reach a hard rule. It covers every vehicle that lands a commit there: a bare `git push` while HEAD is on the default branch, `git push origin HEAD:main`, `git push origin +main`, `git push --all`, and `git push --mirror`, on any remote. Two things are outside it. Committing locally on the default branch is not a push. Merging an approved pull or merge request through `gh pr merge` or `glab mr merge` is a server-side merge, judged by Merge Without Review instead.
environment: **Organization**: an individual developer, working both on personal projects and inside an employer's repositories. Primary use of Claude Code: software development, plus authoring the Claude Code plugins and personal automation in the configuration repo at github.com/bendrucker/claude.
**Source control**: GitHub, under github.com/bendrucker. Repositories owned by `bendrucker` are the user's own. Repositories under any other owner are third-party, whoever granted write access.

**Repository visibility**: repositories owned by `bendrucker` are overwhelmingly public open source, several hundred of them, including the configuration repository this file lives in. Employer repositories are private. Working locally in a checkout says nothing either way. So when visibility decides something (whether a value belongs in a tracked file, what a commit message or pull request body exposes), resolve it instead of inferring it from the name: `gh repo view --json visibility` answers it for a GitHub remote, and it is one call.

**Trusted repo**: a session's repository is frequently a git worktree rather than a primary checkout, living either at `.worktrees/<branch>` inside the repo or in a sibling directory created by the `wt` (Worktrunk) CLI. A worktree is the same repository as the checkout it was created from: its remotes, branches, and history are inside the trust boundary, and `.git` being a file rather than a directory does not make it foreign.

A single session may operate across more than one checkout, because a change often spans a service repository and its configuration repository. A second checkout is inside the trust boundary when it shares a source-control host and owner with the repository the session started in, and outside it otherwise.

**Scratch space**: `tmp/` within a repository and the session's own scratchpad directory under `/tmp/claude-*/` are disposable working areas rather than repository content. `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, and `$TMPDIR` as a whole are shared with other sessions and processes and are not scratch. Neither is `.worktrees/`, which holds real branches with uncommitted work.

**Secrets management**: credentials live in the macOS Keychain, in 1Password, and in per-tool config under `~/.config` and `~/.local`. They are read by the tools that own them and never copied into a repository, a commit, a message, or a network request.
**Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: none configured, and none wanted. Repository contents do not go to public paste, gist, or snippet services.

**CI/CD deploy targets**: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI, driven through the `gh` and `glab` CLIs. Reading run status, job logs, artifacts, pull request and merge request state, and review threads is routine work, not reconnaissance.
allow: Scratch Cleanup: deleting or overwriting files under a repository's `tmp/` directory, or under this session's own scratchpad directory beneath `/tmp/claude-*/`, is routine. Both are disposable by convention, so the usual protection for files that pre-date the session does not apply within them. This does not extend to `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, or `$TMPDIR` as a whole, which other sessions and processes share: a wildcard or age-filtered sweep of those stays blocked.

Worktree Removal: removing a git worktree the session created, through `wt remove` or `git worktree remove`, is routine cleanup rather than destruction of work. A worktree the session did not create may hold another session's uncommitted branch and is not covered. Neither is any removal that forces past a dirty tree (`wt remove --force`, `wt sync --prune --force`, `-F`), whatever created the worktree: the force flag exists to discard uncommitted work.

Stack Restack: `wt sync --push` rebases the session's own stack of dependent topic branches onto their parents and force-pushes each one, which is how a stack stays consistent. This covers only branches the Unowned Force Push rule would treat as owned. It does not cover `wt sync --all`, which reaches every worktree in the repository including branches another session or machine is working on.
soft_deny: Unowned Force Push [named+specifics — **must name:** the branch being force-pushed]: force-pushing (`git push --force`, `--force-with-lease`, or a `+ref` refspec) is allowed on a branch this session owns and blocked on any other. A branch is owned when the transcript shows this session created the commits on it, when the session created the branch or its worktree, or when it is a topic branch of the session's own repository whose pull or merge request lists `bendrucker` as author. A repository's default branch is never owned, and neither is a branch whose commits pre-date the session with no evidence of who wrote them.

Third-Party Public Surface [named+specifics — **must name:** the target repository]: publishing to a repository owned by anyone other than `bendrucker` is blocked, whoever granted write access. It covers opening a pull or merge request, opening an issue or discussion, and commenting on any of them. Each one posts under the user's name in a project that is not theirs, where strangers see a wrong one before it can be retracted. Two tests, either of which puts the target outside. Structural: an explicit destination names something other than the `origin` remote of the session's own repository, whether through `gh pr create --repo`, `gh issue create --repo`, `gh issue comment`, `gh pr comment`, `glab mr create --target-project`, `glab issue create --repo`, a `gh api` or `glab api` write call, or a browser. Implicit: a bare `gh pr create` in a clone whose `origin` is a fork resolves its base to the parent repository, so it targets the parent with no flag at all, and a bare `gh issue create` in that same clone files against the parent too. Forking an outside repository and pushing a branch to that fork is covered as well, since it is the step before the request. Reading is not publishing: viewing, listing, and searching issues, pull requests, and review threads anywhere is routine work. Contributing upstream is fine once the user names the target repository.
